appendix: From here on is the appendix for questions. It holds the basis for every definition and method used in the main deck, the data structure, and the results of the quality checks.
censoring: This slide attacks our own core result (RQ1.1). Under the default definition, 90-day repurchase falls 12.4 points from 43.4% to 31.0% in November 2019, the last cohort whose window ends before the closures. But the March to May 2019 cohorts may be high for two reasons. One is existing customers who had been away for more than six months and slipped through the buffer. The other is seasonality: first-time buyers in March to May hit the June summer sale within 90 days. Extending the buffer to 12 months and starting from the September 2019 cohort, the drop is 4.8 points, from 35.8% to 31.0%. So the accurate statement is that the direction of the drop is certain and its size is between 5 and 12 points. A same-month comparison a year apart (2019-03 vs 2020-03) overlaps with COVID and cannot be used.
corrections: This table is the result of checking, one by one, an outside review a teammate received. Every point in the review was right. 4,101 stores is as of 30 November 2025, while 3,579, 82 and 62 are as of 31 August 2026, so they must not be mixed in one sentence. The 26–30% online share is from after 2020, not the Kaggle period; the official figures for the Kaggle period are 14.5% to 28%. Correcting this makes the gap between sample and group even bigger, which supports the “direction, not level” rule even more strongly. These corrections go into the Phase 4 methodology (sample vs group) and the RQ2.3 wording.
cover: Today’s conclusion is the title: H&M’s problem is less about winning new customers than about getting them to come back a second time. We get there in four steps. First, who H&M is and what it worries about in its own reports. Then we browse our data and find a clue. We turn the clue into questions, pick a method for each, and check four findings one by one. Finally, one proposal per finding and the limits of the analysis. Data and method details are in the appendix.
diagnosis: We checked whether the clue also shows in sales. We split value into four factors and, to keep COVID out, looked only at October 2019 to February 2020. The sample’s value fell 7.5% year on year. Group sales grew 5% in the same months, so the level cannot be carried over, but we can see what moved. Price rose and visit frequency held. What fell was the number of buying customers and how much they buy at once. The split alone cannot tell new from existing customers, but with the clue the problem reads: there are signs that first-time customers return less, and buy less when they do. That gives four questions, answered one by one in the next part.
dictionary: We built the dictionary so teammates would not read the same column in different ways. For example, the Phase 3 draft listed Ladieswear, Divided, Menswear and Baby/Children next to index_name, but those four are values of index_group_name. index_name has 10 values such as Lingeries/Tights and Baby Sizes 50-98, and index_group_name also includes Sport. Membership status and newsletter subscription are snapshots of unknown date, so we did not use them as causes.
exec: This one page is enough on its own. The situation is official figures from H&M’s reports; the problem is what we found in the transaction data. The clearest signal is that new customers come back less. Much of the fall in new-customer counts was an artefact of where the data start; what remains is the drop in new-customer repurchase. All-customer repeat held level with the prior year, and seasonality is not ruled out, so we size it conservatively at 5 points. Closing stores rests on the assumption that customers of a closed store follow it online, and the 2020 temporary shutdown says that assumption did not hold. That was a chain-wide shutdown with reopening expected; whether the same holds for permanent closures of individual stores is an assumption. So the proposals focus on getting customers to come back after the first purchase, and on turning store customers into two-channel customers before stores close. The impact figure is an upper bound; an A/B test will measure the real size.
f1: Each bar is a cohort of new customers who first bought in the same month. 43.4% of the March 2019 cohort bought again within 90 days; for November 2019 it was 31.0%. November is the endpoint because it is the last cohort whose 90-day window ends, in late February 2020, before the store closures. Over the same period H&M group sales grew 4–8% a quarter in local currencies, so even while the company looked healthy, new customers in the sample were coming back less. The size is best stated as 5 to 12 points: early cohorts may include lapsed existing customers, and with a 12-month buffer the drop is 4.8 points. With only one clean year, seasonality is not ruled out. We also tested it: the nine clean cohorts differ significantly by chi-square, and a logistic regression controlling basket, channel, age and line still gives 43.0% to 31.6%. It is not just a change in mix.
f2: The left panel is the cumulative return rate from survival analysis. Customers who had not returned by the end of the data are not counted as failures; they stay in the risk set only up to that point. The right panel is a conditional probability. A customer not back by day 30 has a 10.6% chance of returning in the next 30 days; by day 90 it is 6.8%, and by day 270 about 3.6%. After day 270 it flattens at 3.4–3.7%. In practice, the window to act is 30 to 90 days after the first purchase. Note that the curve shows when customers return, not when they are lost for good. For reference, across all customers including existing ones, the median gap from first to second purchase is 44 days, and the median gap between consecutive purchases is 22 days. The method is summarised in Appendix H.
f3: The line I wrote in the Phase 4 outline, “basket size, not the product,” was too strong. At 90 days the spread across product groups (29.2–38.1%, 8.9 points) is about the same as the spread across basket sizes (8.3 points). The difference is consistency. Basket size rises in order from 1 item to 2–3, 4–6 and 7+, at both 90 and 365 days. Product groups narrow to a 5.8-point spread at 365 days and their ranking changes. Swimwear is first at 90 days, most likely a seasonal effect: spring and summer first-time buyers hit the June sale. On causality we must be careful. Customers with big first baskets may already be keen on H&M, so interventions such as bundle offers have to be checked with an A/B test. The method is summarised in Appendix H. Logistic regression controls the other factors: a first basket of 7+ items has 1.37 times the odds of repurchase of a single item, 33.5% → 40.8% adjusted. Explanatory power is low: this model shows the direction and size of a difference, it does not predict who returns. And it is an adjusted association, not an intervention effect.
f4: Supporting analysis A. This looks like the second way the customer count shrinks. Customers who used only stores, or only online, in the first year of the data: close to half bought nothing at all the following year. Only 11.4% of customers who used both channels bought nothing the next year. That is lapsing, not permanent loss: they may have returned after the data ends. The value gap is large too: an omni customer is worth 3.4 times an online-only customer and 6.2 times a store-only customer. But this comparison is not causal. Customers who already like H&M may be the ones who came to use both channels. So we do not claim that switching customers to omni raises their value; we propose testing a conversion programme on customers of stores due to close. For reference, the main reason online orders are bigger than store orders is the number of items per order (4.09 vs 2.55). The method is summarised in Appendix H. Here the test changed the story. Raw, single-channel customers have about 7 times the lapse odds of omni customers. But they buy far less to begin with: median year-1 purchases are 7 for omni, 1 for online only and 2 for store only. Controlling purchases, months observed and age, the odds ratio falls to about 1.3, and only about 5 of the 36 points stay with the channel. So we size proposal ③ small and test it.
f5: The March to May 2020 closures were not a randomised experiment, but they were an outside shock customers did not choose, so we treat them as a natural experiment. The baseline is the key. On its own, “55.4% of store-only customers bought again after reopening” cannot be interpreted. A group built the same way one year earlier bought at 47.3% in the same season. So store-only customers actually came back more than usual, which looks like pent-up demand being released. Online-only and omni customers are almost identical to their baselines. Limits: this baseline comparison is a simplified difference-in-differences and does not control for other changes between 2019 and 2020, such as a different mix of new customers. And because the closures were temporary, carrying this over to permanent closures needs care. The method is summarised in Appendix H. The difference by channel type is significant by chi-square, with a medium effect size. The +8.1 pp after reopening has a 95% CI of 7.8–8.4, though 67k customers sit in both years’ groups, so the samples are not fully independent.
f6: In Phases 2–3 we wrote that shoppers aged 55 and over rely more on stores, but the full data does not show that. The in-store share is lowest at 25–34 and rises on both sides in a U shape; 55–64 is actually lower than 16–24 and 45–54. Only the 65+ group supports the claim. And 65+ is a small group with low value per customer, so rather than basing store decisions on this group alone, it fits the data better to propose bridges such as click-and-collect and in-store returns. These shares are by transaction row; recomputing by value or by customer may shift the figures slightly. These shares are by transaction row. The method is summarised in Appendix H. Age differences are statistically significant, but in an ANOVA of each customer’s in-store share, age explains only 0.2% of the variation. With a sample this large, small differences come out significant. So prioritising 65+ is only a supporting argument.
impact: These are the numbers behind why the proposals are worth trying. Among 290,000 new customers who first bought between March and September 2019, the first purchase was almost the same whether or not they came back. But those who came back once within 90 days had a first-year value of 0.49, 2.7 times the 0.18 of those who did not. What makes the difference is the second purchase, not the first. So each 1-point rise in 90-day repurchase adds about 1% to a new cohort’s first-year value, and since new customers made 28.4% of the last year’s value, about 0.3% of total sample value. Getting back to the September 2019 level, about 5 points higher, would add about 1.4%. These are ratios inside the sample, so we do not compare them directly with H&M group sales growth. And value is a sum of transformed prices, not profit, so ROI net of cost has to be measured in the A/B test. These figures are an upper bound that assumes customers pulled back by an offer spend like those who return on their own, and that the sample’s ratios apply to the group.
limits: Putting the limits up front, rather than hiding them, makes the analysis more credible. The top two rows, sample representativeness and the lack of data after 2020, set the scope of the conclusions. Because of them we do not say “H&M’s repurchase rate is X percent”; we say “in this sample, new-customer repurchase weakened cohort after cohort, and it is concentrated in the first 90 days.” Because prices are transformed, the ROI of the proposals needs an assumption to convert using report figures, which we will give as a range in the next step. Two more: with one clean year of new cohorts the drop could be seasonal, and all-customer repeat held level with the prior year, so we narrow the claim to new customers’ second purchase.
methods: Rigour here means the simplest method that fits the question, not the most complex model. For repurchase timing, survival analysis is standard: counting customers who have not returned by the end of the data as failures understates repurchase for recent cohorts. BTYD models such as BG/NBD are the standard for forecasting customer lifetime value, but our question is to diagnose when and who comes back less, and with transformed prices, money forecasts mean little, so we left it as an extension. Ideally the closure effect would use difference-in-differences, but there is no data on unclosed control markets, so we used the same customer groups in the same months a year earlier as the baseline. That is a simplified DiD, not a causal estimate.
next: We do not yet know Δp, the rise in 90-day repurchase an intervention can achieve, so we give scenarios rather than one number. Because prices are transformed, the value of the second purchase V has to be converted using H&M’s reported revenue and customer counts, and that assumption is stated in the table. The point to stress is that today’s conclusion is a decision to test, not a decision to roll out. What the data tells us is where to place the experiments.
process: The biggest risk in exploratory analysis is what Gelman and Loken call the garden of forking paths. Slice the data enough ways and a plausible pattern will appear by chance, and it is tempting to present it as if it had been the hypothesis all along (HARKing, Kerr 1998). We reduced this in three ways. First, definitions such as occasion and new customer were set before looking at results. Second, research questions RQ1.1–2.3 were fixed in Phase 2. Third, the workbook’s L_Lineage sheet records which code and table every figure came from, so anyone can reproduce it.
proposal: Each proposal answers one finding directly. First, the chance of a customer coming back drops sharply after 90 days, so the prompt has to land between day 30 and day 60. Before day 30 many customers would return anyway, which wastes the spend; after day 90 is too late. Second, repurchase rises step by step with first-basket size, so we grow the first basket with outfit bundles or a free-shipping threshold. Third, in the 2020 temporary shutdown store customers did not move online; assuming the same holds for permanent closures, before a closure we turn them into two-channel customers through app sign-up, click-and-collect and in-store returns. The 65+ group has the highest in-store share, so it comes first. All three rest on correlation, so we measure the real effect in a test before scaling.
quality: The last row matters most. Some Phase 1–2 figures came from pd.read_csv(nrows=1_000_000). The file is sorted by date, so the first million rows were not a random sample but 22 days, from 20 September to 11 October 2018. Computing on that range reproduces the submitted figures exactly (214,936 customers, 66.3% online). A random sample would have given about 499,000 customers. All later figures were recomputed on the full data.
refs: Every figure can be rebuilt from the code in the repo. The workbook’s L_Lineage sheet records which function and table produced each figure. Figures computed new for this deck are the 12-month new-customer buffer sensitivity check (35.8% → 31.0%), the impact sizing (first-year value 0.49 vs 0.18; 28.4% share), and the review checks (price percentiles, index values, in-store share by age). Of the outside sources cited in the submission, the Measure Protocol panel, Gallo’s 5–25 times and the Fortune article have no copy in the repo, so reopen the originals before using them in Phase 4.
schema: This is close to a star schema: transactions are the fact table, customers and articles the dimension tables. The key point is that one transaction row is one item, not one receipt. There is no receipt number or time, so we grouped a customer’s purchases on the same day into one purchase occasion. That definition is the base unit for repurchase, basket size and purchase gaps. 1,362,281 customers appear in transactions, and 104,547 articles were sold. Buying the same item twice on one day repeats the row, since there is no quantity column, and article_id is read as text to keep its leading zero.
situation: This is the symptom we started from. After growth of 12% in 2021 and 6% in 2022, sales effectively stopped for three years from 2023: −1%, 1%, 2%. Over the same period stores fell from 4,801 to 4,101, a drop of 700. Management’s response is store optimisation, which assumes customers of closed stores move online. Our project’s two issues, retention and channel shift, come straight from these two questions. The store bars start at zero, so the 15% drop looks as large as it is.
sources: H&M released the Kaggle data itself but did not say which markets or customers it drew. So we do not assume it represents the whole group. The reports, by contrast, cover the whole group but have no customer-level data. The two sources complement each other rather than substitute, and this split is the starting point for the time-gap handling and validity discussion.
summary: In one sentence: repeat visits by H&M’s new customers were already weakening in 2019, while the company was still growing; customers who come back mostly do so within the first 90 days, and the size of the first basket is what moves that chance. On the channel side, store customers waited through the closures and returned to stores rather than moving online. Value is relative, because the price column is transformed and is not real currency.
timeline: This picture is the project’s biggest methodological issue. The data that shows customer behaviour ends in September 2020, but the flat sales and store cuts that worry management stand out from 2023. The two sources truly overlap only in FY2019 and the first three quarters of FY2020, seven quarters in all. In that overlap we can line up the sample and the group on the same calendar; joining across the gap needs an assumption. The next two slides cover that assumption and how far it can be trusted.
timeuse: Why direction and not level: the sample’s online share is 70.4% by row and 75.6% by value, while H&M reported 14.5% for FY2018 and 28% for FY2020 in the same period. The FY2019 report does not state a share. The gap means the sample leans heavily towards online members. Also, from October 2019 to February 2020 the sample’s value fell year on year while group sales rose. So a sample level, such as a 31.0% repurchase rate, cannot be stated as an H&M-wide figure. What we can state is the direction and relative difference from comparing cohorts within the same sample. Linking 2019 to 2025 is a hypothesis, and we wrote down the condition under which it would be judged wrong.
units: Before the findings, the definitions. The Phase 3 feedback asked us to be clear about how we count new customers, repurchase and baskets. A basket is the items in one occasion; lapsed means no purchase in the next 12 months, and permanent loss cannot be seen in this data. Value is a sum of transformed prices, not profit or margin. Why occasions: with no receipt number, a customer who bought five items at once shows up as five rows. Counting repurchase by rows would wrongly treat the second item bought the same day as a repurchase. Grouping by customer and day removes that problem. Occasions where the customer used both store and online on the same day (94,278, 1%) are flagged separately. The six-month buffer in the new-customer definition and the population limit are explained on the censoring slide.
validity: The last line answers the Law of Large Numbers paragraph that was going to go into the submission. It is true that a large sample shrinks sampling error, but only when the sample is drawn at random from the population. This data leans towards online members, and that lean stays even with 30 million rows. So we rate the risk to statistical conclusions as low and the risk to external and temporal validity as high. That is why our conclusions stay at comparisons between cohorts and at direction.
feedback: Phases 1 to 3 scored 45 out of 50, and the feedback was not to draw conclusions beyond what the data show. The table shows how we acted on each point. In particular, every analysis slide now carries a label at the top right, so you can see which claims come straight from the data and which are estimates or assumptions. Next, how we handled the time gap.
calc: Open this slide when asked how a number was computed. Three points. First, items bought on the same day count as one purchase. Second, the repurchase denominator only includes customers whose first N days fall inside the data, so recent customers who have not come back yet are not counted as lost. Third, time to repurchase uses Kaplan–Meier survival analysis: customers not back yet stay at risk only until the data ends, so they are neither dropped nor counted as failures. The next-30-day chance is conditional: of customers not back by day t, the share who return in the next 30 days. The shutdown comparison uses the same period a year earlier, a simplified difference-in-differences, so we do not call it causal. Supporting B is by transaction row; averaged per customer the values change, but 65+ is still the highest.
intro: Before we start, three quick questions. Hands up if you bought from H&M in the past year. In a store, or in the app or online? And who bought again after that? That third question is today’s topic. H&M is one of the world’s largest fashion houses, with the purpose of liberating fashion for the many, and runs brands such as COS, Weekday and ARKET alongside H&M. Net sales last year were about SEK 228 billion. H&M sells in 81 markets through about 4,100 stores, and just over 30% of sales are online. More than 200 million customers are in its loyalty programme. Yet the store count fell by more than a thousand, from 5,076 at the end of 2019 to 4,023 in the third quarter of 2026.
concerns: These come straight from H&M’s own reports. The 2025 annual report says consumers are more price-conscious and inclined to change. The Q2 2025 report admits that closing stores cuts short-term sales: with 4% fewer stores, growth fell from 3% to 1%. At the same time, H&M says the store matters more than ever. In 2018 the CEO cited more returning customers, without a number. We pulled 952 statements from 43 reports: member counts appear, but no repurchase or lapse rate anywhere. So we checked in the transaction data whether customers really come back.
datacard: This is the data we have: 31.8 million rows that H&M released on Kaggle, one row per item bought, over two years from September 2018. There is almost nothing missing, but four things matter. FN and Active in the customer table are 65% blank, but their only value is 1, so we read a blank as 0. With no receipt ID, we group a customer’s purchases on one day into one purchase. Channels 1 and 2 are undefined, so we assume 2 is online. Prices are transformed, so we read them only as ratios. And with no store, country or cost data, this data cannot speak to individual store closures or margins.
browse1: The first thing we looked at was the distribution, because an average hides it. We grouped customers by how often they bought in two years. A third bought exactly once and made only 4.8% of value. The 7.8% who bought 20 or more times made 38.5%. That raised the first question: if so many customers come once and stop, how many first-time customers come back?
browse2: So we grouped first-time customers by the month of their first purchase. On the left, new customers seem to halve, from 51,000 to 25,000 a month. But part of that is an artefact. The data start in September 2018, so spring 2019 “new” customers can include existing customers returning after a long gap; those are the light bars. On the right, the share buying again next month still falls after September 2019, from 16.0% to 12.7% in January 2020. February 2020 is left out because its next month is the shutdown. That is a signal that repurchase is weakening. It is a rough calendar-month measure, so in the next part we measure it properly.
methodsel: Having turned the clue into questions, we followed the course’s method-selection guide for each one. First the outcome, its type, and what one row is. Where the outcome is yes or no, such as whether a customer repurchased or bought the next year, we start with a chi-square test and then use binary logistic regression to control for other factors. When customers return is beyond the guide: follow-up differs by customer, so a fixed-window logistic model cannot answer it, and we use survival analysis. For a numeric outcome across three or more groups, like in-store share, we use ANOVA, and a rank test because the distribution is skewed. With hundreds of thousands of customers, p values are almost all near zero, so we read effect sizes and confidence intervals.
explain: Before the findings, four methods in plain terms. A cohort repurchase rate groups customers who first bought in the same month and counts how many come back: 43 of 100 March 2019 newcomers bought again within 90 days, so 43%. Survival analysis updates the share not back yet, day by day, and keeps customers in the count until their follow-up ends, so follow-up can differ. An odds ratio says how many times the odds are, all else equal; the adjusted rate turns it back into a percentage. And with hundreds of thousands of customers, p values are all near zero, so we read effect sizes on a 0 to 1 scale.
browse0: Before anything else we plotted each column. Top left: value peaks in June, dips in the March 2020 shutdown and recovers online in April. Top right: the median customer is 32, with two peaks, early twenties and late forties. Bottom left: 70% of rows are channel 2, while the group sells just over 30% online, so this sample leans online. Bottom right: two thirds of rows are womenswear. We keep these skews in mind before generalising to the whole group.
